response.text:
Henry Adams begins life in 1838 under the shadow of Boston’s State House and the longer shadow of the Adams name, divided early between the austerity of Beacon Hill winters and the sensual liberty of Quincy summers. His childhood unfolds among patriarchs, pulpits, and politics—his grandfather John Quincy Adams a living monument; his mother’s Maryland heritage a faint undertone of otherness—so that from the first he breathes a double atmosphere. The Boston of unitarian rectitude and State Street calculation teaches him suspicion of power, yet educates him in salon talk and civic duty; his earliest moral lessons are already ambivalent. By 1848 he watches the old order dimly crack: J.Q. Adams dies, Free-Soil politics ignite, and Charles Sumner, whom the boy will revere and then oppose, emerges as a heroic lodestar.

School in Boston and even Harvard (1854–58) fail him; the curriculum seems a museum of dead forms, and the most living instruction comes at family tables and in the company of men like Lowell. A foray to Berlin evaporates in pedantry, punctured only by unexpected awakenings—the music of Beethoven penetrating his unconscious, the German gymnasium teaching him the hard limits of memory. Rome in 1859 descends like revelation: medieval stones, papal ritual, and the living sorcery of unity intoxicate him even as Garibaldi’s campaigns argue another religion of force. He returns through Paris in 1860, where he refuses French seductions and resolves to report on his time.

The Civil War makes him private secretary to his father, then Minister to Britain, and London becomes his great school. Diplomacy teaches him that statesmanship is geometry under fog: his father must counter Palmerston’s genial cunning and Lord Russell’s shifting evasions, and the son learns to take notes, hold his tongue, and decode power. The Trent Affair, the Alabama claims, the furious fight over the Laird rams—here Adams sees law collide with interest and language conceal motive until, by relentless pressure and patient maneuver, the rams are stopped and a discreet victory for American neutrality is won. London society entertains, resents, and educates him by indifference; he measures his ignorance against English complacency and files it as data.

After Appomattox he drifts between Boston’s granite certainties and Washington’s fluid intrigues, and in the 1870s he tries both journalism and the classroom, failing amiably at each. Harvard gives him a pulpit he distrusts, and the students teach him more than he teaches them; so he returns to self-education—the kind that begins at Mont-Saint-Michel and kneels under Chartres’ glass, seeking in stone and light the logic of a century that made unity almost a physical force. He writes his medieval book to fix a unit—how the twelfth-century mind cohered around the Virgin—and watches the nineteenth century answer with centrifugal modernity. The true teachers become friends: Clarence King, arctic genius of geology; John Hay, urban and humane, who will carry American diplomacy over its shoals; and the artists—Saint-Gaudens, La Farge—who translate energy into form.

Then Chicago’s Fair of 1893 throws him under the pulsing armature of the dynamo, and Paris’s Exposition of 1900 sets him in a new nave: one illumined by incandescent bulbs instead of stained glass. He feels the dynamo as a moral force, a blunt, inexhaustible infinity that shrugs at theology and answers questions with motion; against it he sets the Virgin of Chartres, symbol of unity, as personal and persuasive as the new machine is anonymous and vast. The Panic of 1893 strips him of illusions and money; science strips him of order, as new rays and elusive atoms mock the old Euclidian comfort. He wanders to Norway, Russia, and Germany, groping for measures of race inertia and the frustrate velocities of empire, and tests the twentieth-century American against both.

Back in Washington, he sees Hay elevate the State Department into a gentleman’s workshop, regrets how the Senate still scatters treaties like so many flies, and privately rejoices that the Open Door survives mass and appetite long enough to become policy. Around him acceleration becomes palpable: coal tonnages doubling by decades, steam multiplying into steel, electricity becoming a second sun. From this pressure he fashions a makeshift law—that history is the economy of force, and its curve one of relentless acceleration, measurable in coal, in ships’ horsepower, in nerves racked by speed. He reads Karl Pearson and Poincaré and hears, beneath their equations, the whisper that order is a convenience; he accepts that nature’s grammar admits contradiction and that science has sailed beyond unity into seas where even the compass lies.

Late friendships burn with compact brilliance: Saint-Gaudens models heads against time; Hay reads the newspapers’ bulletins of the world with a genial scorn that masks foreknowledge; King, ideally begun and tragically pursued, fades like a great comet into the western haze. The deaths come: King first; then, after a European cure that gives only the appetite for conversation, Hay. Each summons Adams nearer the garden wall and teaches him twice to hold silence. The Republic, in Roosevelt’s charge, tries to throttle trusts with a will and a smile, and Adams, admiring the energy but doubting the calculus, prefers to note the pressure gauge rather than steady the piston.

At last the experiment in self-education arrives at its formulae: Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres for unity, The Virgin and the Dynamo for multiplicity; a Dynamic Theory of History that assumes man is a captured meteor, dragged by new forces into an orbit beyond his old thought; a Law of Acceleration that predicts perihelion soon, perhaps catastrophe, certainly a new equilibrium beyond present senses. By his own measure, his education ends in recognized ignorance and a last, sardonic hope that the child of 1900 will learn to think in complexities and survive. Near the close he sits again on the steps of Ara Cœli, a tired pilgrim who has prayed before two altars, taken soundings in two oceans, and learned chiefly that force educates, unity consoles, and silence at the end is the most intelligent speech left to man.
